title: What Do Christians Owe the City They Live In?
subtitle: What it means to be a citizen of an earthly city while belonging first to another. Augustine's two cities, the call to seek the welfare of the place where God has put you, the common good above the tribe, and a public faith that refuses to be captured by any party, on the left or the right.

parts.title: The Allegiance You Did Not Notice Changing
parts.body:
Somewhere along the way, your politics started to feel more important than your faith, and you did not notice it happening. You would deny it, of course. If asked, you would say Christ is Lord and the kingdom comes first. But watch where the heat is. Watch what raises your pulse, what you cannot stop scrolling, what makes you suspicious of a brother who votes the other way, what you would actually argue about at the table. The honest test is not what you confess on Sunday. It is what you are gripped by on Tuesday, and for many of us the grip of party has quietly grown stronger than the grip of the gospel, while we went on calling ourselves Christians first.

It happened the way these things always happen, by degrees and for good reasons. The issues are real. The stakes feel high. And the machinery of the age is built to make you feel that everything hangs on the next election, that the other side is not merely wrong but evil, that to hold back your full allegiance is to betray the cause. So you gave a little more of your heart, and a little more, until somewhere the party stopped being a flawed instrument you used with one eye open and became a home you defended, a tribe you belonged to, a thing you were no longer free to criticize. The conversion was so gradual you never felt the floor move.

And here is what you have learned to do with your faith in the meantime. You have learned to use it. You reach for Scripture when it arms your side and grow strangely quiet when it indicts your side. You can quote the Bible at length against the other tribe's sins and you fall silent on the sins your tribe has made its peace with. Your faith has become, without your deciding it, the chaplain of your politics, blessing what you already wanted, sanctifying the conclusions you reached on other grounds. The tail is wagging the dog, and the dog is sure it is in charge.

The watching skeptic sees this with perfect clarity, which is part of why he stays away. He has noticed that he can predict almost everything a given Christian believes about God, sin, mercy, and the poor simply by learning which way that Christian votes. He has concluded, not unreasonably, that the faith is a costume the politics wears, that the praying is downstream of the party, that Jesus has been enlisted as a mascot for a tribe he never joined. When the church's public witness is indistinguishable from a voting bloc, the gospel looks like ideology in a stained-glass frame, and the skeptic is right to refuse it.

I am not writing this from a safe distance. I have felt the pull, the satisfying certainty of the tribe, the small contempt for the people on the other side, the way the heart warms to the verse that wounds my opponent and cools toward the one that wounds me. The capture is not something that happens to other Christians. It is the constant temptation of every believer who has a public life, and the first step toward freedom is the hardest, which is to admit that on this ground my heart is already half-claimed by a master other than the Lord.

parts.title: Why the Kingdom Will Not Share a Throne
parts.body:
Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, Jesus said, and to God the things that are God's, and the whole weight of the saying is in the second clause. He grants the earthly authority its real but limited due, the coin that bears its image, and then he reserves for God the thing that bears God's image, which is you, entire, undivided. The kingdom of God will not share a throne. It does not ask for a slice of your allegiance to sit beside your party and your nation. It asks for the throne, and a faith that has handed half the throne to a political tribe is not a balanced faith but a divided one, and Jesus was clear about what becomes of a house divided.

The first stake is idolatry, which is the precise word for what happens when a good thing takes God's place. Politics is a good thing, a real arena of love for neighbor, and that is exactly why it makes such an effective idol, because idols are never made of obviously evil materials but of good things loved too much. The nation is a good thing and becomes an idol when it claims ultimate loyalty. The party is a good thing and becomes an idol when it becomes the lens through which you read even the Bible. Justice is a good thing and becomes an idol when it is severed from mercy and worshiped as the whole. The most dangerous idols in a believer's life are not the crude ones but the noble ones, the causes so good that we cannot imagine loving them too much, and political idolatry is the most respectable idolatry available to the modern Christian.

The second stake is the body, the church itself, which the partisan capture tears apart from the inside. The New Testament's astonishment is that in Christ the dividing walls are down, that Jew and Gentile, slave and free, the people who had every earthly reason to hate each other, now sit at one table as one family. The American tribes have rebuilt the wall straight down the middle of the church. We have allowed the partisan division of the nation to become the partisan division of the body of Christ, so that brothers and sisters who share a baptism cannot share a meal without the politics rising like a wall between them. When the church sorts itself by party, it denies the gospel it preaches, because the gospel's first proof is a reconciled people, and a people who cannot be reconciled across a voting line have un-preached the gospel with their own seating chart.

And the third stake is the witness, which is the church's whole reason to be public at all. We were sent to be salt and light, a city on a hill, a people whose common life makes the watching world wonder what God they serve. But a church captured by a party has nothing to show the world that the world does not already have. It offers the same anger, the same contempt, the same certainty that the other side is the enemy, only with a verse attached. The skeptic does not need the church to teach him how to be a partisan. He has cable news for that. He needs the church to show him the one thing the political order cannot produce, a people who love across the lines that divide everyone else, and when the church fails to be that, it forfeits the only public witness worth having and confirms the skeptic in his suspicion that the gospel changes nothing it cannot already find at a rally.

parts.title: Two Cities, One Welfare, and the Refusal of the Tribe
parts.body:
Begin with the deepest pattern the Bible gives for the Christian's public life, the pattern of the exile, because it reframes everything. The people of God in Scripture are repeatedly a people living in a city that is not finally their own. Abraham was a sojourner. Israel was a stranger in Egypt and then an exile in Babylon. The church in the New Testament is called a colony of heaven, its true citizenship in another country, its members sojourners and exiles passing through. This is not a counsel of withdrawal. It is a posture, the posture of a people who hold a real but penultimate stake in the earthly city, who can love the place without worshiping it, work for its good without staking their souls on it, because their final hope is fixed somewhere the next election cannot touch.

From that posture comes the single most important political instruction in the Old Testament, given to exiles in a hostile empire. Through the prophet Jeremiah, God tells the captives in Babylon not to withdraw and not to revolt, but to build houses, plant gardens, raise families, and, most strikingly, to seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the Lord on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare. Read that again, because it dismantles both of our reflexes. God tells his people to seek the good of Babylon, the pagan empire that conquered them, the regime they had every reason to hate. Not to conquer it, not to flee it, not to baptize it, but to seek its welfare, to bend their lives toward the flourishing of the actual place where God had put them, including the neighbors who did not share their faith. The common good is not a modern liberal invention. It is a command given to exiles, and we are exiles still.

Augustine gathered all of this into the great image that has shaped Christian political thought ever since. Writing as the Roman world collapsed around him in the early fifth century, in his vast work The City of God, he saw that human history is the story of two cities intermingled, the city of God and the city of man, built by two loves. The earthly city is built by the love of self extending to contempt of God. The heavenly city is built by the love of God extending to forgetting of self. The two cities are not two institutions you can point to, not the church and the state, but two orientations of the heart, mixed together in every nation and even in every congregation, and they will not be finally separated until the end. The Christian lives as a citizen of the heavenly city while sojourning in the earthly one, using its peace, obeying its just laws, contributing to its order, but never confusing it with the Kingdom, never giving it the love that belongs to God alone.

This is why Augustine could say that the earthly city's peace is a real good that the Christian should desire and serve, and also that it is not the true peace, not the final city, not the thing worth dying for in the way the Kingdom is worth dying for. The believer can be the best citizen Babylon has, precisely because he is not finally a citizen of Babylon. His hope does not ride on the city's fortunes, and so he can serve it freely, criticize it honestly, and love it without the desperation that turns politics into religion. The man whose whole hope is in the earthly city will do anything to win, lie, hate, justify any means, because for him the election really is the last judgment. The man whose hope is in the heavenly city is free to lose, free to be fair to his opponent, free to tell the truth even when it costs his side, because he already knows how the real story ends.

And Scripture refuses, again and again, to let the people of God be captured by a faction. Joshua meets the commander of the Lord's army before the battle of Jericho and asks the decisive question, are you for us or for our adversaries. The answer is the answer to all our partisan questions. No, comes the reply, but as commander of the army of the Lord I have now come. God does not take a side in the human war. He summons both sides to his side. The prophets indict Israel as fiercely as they indict the nations, and more so, because judgment begins with the household of God. Jesus chose as disciples both Matthew the tax collector, a collaborator with the Roman occupation, and Simon the Zealot, a member of the party sworn to overthrow it by violence, and made them sit at one table for three years. He did not resolve their politics. He relativized them. He put them both under a Lord whose Kingdom made their factions look small.

So the New Testament gives the believer a posture toward the earthly authority that no party can claim. Honor the emperor, Peter writes, and the emperor at the time was Nero. Pray for kings and all in authority, Paul writes, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life. Be subject to the governing authorities, and in the same breath the early church says we must obey God rather than men when the two collide, and goes to its death rather than burn the pinch of incense to Caesar as lord. There is the whole shape of it. Real honor for the earthly city, real participation in its common good, real subjection to its just authority, and an absolute refusal to give it the worship that belongs to God alone. The Christian citizen is the most loyal and the least owned person in the room, and that combination is exactly what the partisan age cannot understand and most needs to see.

parts.title: The Church and the City Through the Centuries
parts.body:
The early church worked out its political theology in the shadow of an empire that demanded worship, and its answer set the pattern for everything after. The Christians were the best of citizens and the worst of subjects, paying their taxes, praying for the emperor, serving their neighbors in the plagues when the pagans fled, and yet refusing the one thing Rome most wanted, the confession that Caesar is Lord. The Letter to Diognetus, written in the second century, described them exactly. They dwell in their own countries, but only as sojourners. Every foreign land is to them a homeland, and every homeland a foreign land. They obey the established laws and surpass the laws in their own lives. They love everyone and are persecuted by everyone. They were the soul of the city without being captured by it, and they died rather than collapse the difference between honoring Caesar and worshiping him.

Augustine, watching Rome fall in 410, gave the church the framework it has used ever since. Pagans blamed the catastrophe on the abandonment of the old gods for Christianity, and Augustine answered with The City of God, arguing that no earthly city, not even eternal Rome, was the Kingdom of God, that all earthly cities rise and fall, and that the people of God must never tie their hope to any of them. He cut the cord between the gospel and the empire at the very moment the empire was dying, and in doing so he freed the church to survive the death of every political order it would ever inhabit. The Christian who has read Augustine does not panic when his nation declines, because he never believed his nation was the Kingdom.

The medieval church then spent a thousand years working out, often badly, the relation between the two swords, the spiritual and the temporal, the church and the crown. At its worst it collapsed the two cities into one, baptized the empire, and persecuted in the name of Christ, forgetting Augustine's warning that the city of God and the city of man remain mixed until the end. At its best it kept alive the conviction that there is an authority above the king, that the ruler is under the law and under God, a conviction that would later feed the whole tradition of limited government and the rule of law. The same centuries that produced the church's political idolatry also preserved the seed of the church's political freedom, the refusal to let any king be God.

The Reformation reopened the question and answered it in rival ways that still divide Protestants. Luther distinguished two kingdoms, the spiritual realm of the gospel and the temporal realm of the sword, and warned against confusing them, though his framework could tilt toward leaving the temporal realm alone. Calvin and the Reformed tradition pressed for the active transformation of the public order under God, sometimes fruitfully and sometimes in the direction of a theocracy that forgot the lesson of the two cities. The Anabaptists withdrew from the sword altogether, bearing a costly witness to the strangeness of the Kingdom and sometimes a separatism that abandoned the neighbor in the city. Each of these is still a live option in the church, and each captures something real about the believer's relation to the public square.

The modern centuries gave both the worst betrayals and the clearest recoveries. The German church in the 1930s split, and the part that fused the gospel with the nation and the Fuhrer showed the world the full horror of political idolatry, while the Confessing Church, in the Barmen Declaration of 1934, drafted largely by Karl Barth, said the thing the captured church could not. Jesus Christ is the one Word of God whom we have to trust and obey, and the church rejects the false doctrine that it should hand itself over to any other lord. Dietrich Bonhoeffer paid for that confession with his life. In the same century, the American civil rights movement showed the church at its public best, when Martin Luther King and the black church brought the prophets into the street, not to capture a party but to summon the whole nation to a justice it had betrayed, calling America back to its own founding promise on explicitly Christian grounds. The lesson of the long history is consistent. When the church marries the party, it dies, and takes its witness down with it. When the church keeps its first allegiance to the Kingdom, it is free to love the city, serve the common good, and tell the nation the truth no party will pay it to tell.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: The nature of citizenship, the common good, and political tribalism are among the most examined subjects in modern thought, and the believer has nothing to fear from honest students of how human beings organize their public life. All truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of politics carries a hidden picture of the human person, and the picture is where the matter is won or lost.

secular.source: The moral psychology of political tribalism
secular.author: Jonathan Haidt
secular.whatItGetsRight: Haidt demonstrated that political conviction runs far less on reason than we pretend, that we reach our positions by intuition and tribal loyalty and then recruit arguments to defend them, and that the righteous mind binds us into groups and blinds us to the humanity of the other side. He showed that left and right are each tuned to real moral goods the other neglects, and that our certainty about our opponents' wickedness is largely an illusion produced by the way groups form around sacred values. This is a precise account of how political idolatry actually captures a mind.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Haidt describes the mechanism of the captured heart with great accuracy and cannot name its root or supply its cure. Scripture agrees that we rationalize, that the heart leads and the reason follows, and goes deeper, calling this not merely tribal wiring but the bent of a fallen heart that loves itself and its own and resists the God who judges all sides. Haidt can help you see your bias. He cannot give you a loyalty higher than the tribe, and without a higher throne the de-biased mind simply finds a more sophisticated way to serve itself. Only allegiance to a Lord above every faction can free a person from the gravity Haidt so clearly maps.

secular.source: Theories of the common good and civic republicanism
secular.author: Michael Sandel and the communitarians
secular.whatItGetsRight: Sandel and the communitarian thinkers recovered, against a thin individualism, the older conviction that a good society needs more than rights and markets, that citizens owe one another a shared concern for the common good, and that a republic depends on virtues and loyalties that mere self-interest cannot supply. They saw that a people reduced to consumers and rights-bearers cannot sustain a common life, and that politics must aim at the good we share and not only the goods we each pursue. This recovers something the gospel always assumed, that we are made for one another.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Sandel reaches toward the common good by reason and arrives near the prophets without their foundation. Scripture grounds the common good not in civic sentiment but in creation, that we are made in the image of one God and for the love of neighbor, and it names what communitarianism cannot, the self-love that makes even the pursuit of the common good a contest for whose vision of the good will rule. A philosophy can describe the shared good. It cannot produce the people humble enough to seek it together, and the Bible knows that the common good is finally impossible without the reordering of the heart that only grace performs.

secular.source: The research on polarization and social fracture
secular.author: Robert Putnam and the political scientists
secular.whatItGetsRight: Putnam documented the collapse of the civic and associational life that once knit Americans together across their differences, and later scholars charted how affective polarization has turned political opponents into perceived enemies, how we increasingly sort ourselves into separate worlds that never meet. They showed, with data, that the bonds which let a divided people remain one people have frayed, and that the resulting tribalism is corrosive to the very possibility of a shared common life. This is the social face of the capture Scripture warns against.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The scientists measure the fracture and cannot heal it, because their tools can describe a broken community but not create a reconciled one. Scripture affirms the diagnosis and supplies what the data cannot, a body in which the deepest human divisions are actually overcome, not by better civics but by a shared Lord who has torn down the dividing wall. The political scientist can map the gap between the tribes. Only the gospel claims to put former enemies at one table and make them family, and the church, when it is faithful, is meant to be the living rebuttal of the polarization the scholars so accurately describe.

secular.source: The liberal account of religion and the public square
secular.author: John Rawls and political liberalism
secular.whatItGetsRight: Rawls and the liberal tradition wrestled honestly with how a society of deep disagreement can live together in peace, proposing that citizens restrain their appeals to their own comprehensive convictions and reason from values all can share. This protects the religious minority from coercion, guards against the establishment of any one faith by force, and reflects a real wisdom about the danger of using state power to impose ultimate beliefs, a danger the church learned the hard way across its own history of persecution.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Rawls protects against one danger and creates another, asking believers to leave their deepest reasons at the door of the public square, which no honest person can do and which secretly privileges one set of convictions while pretending to be neutral. Scripture does not let the Christian bracket his faith, for the same Lord rules the public square and the private heart, and the prophets spoke to kings in the name of God, not in the name of values all could share. The believer enters public life neither to coerce nor to hide, but to bear witness, to seek the common good openly as a follower of Christ, neither establishing the faith by the sword nor amputating it at the curb.

secular.source: Critiques of Christian nationalism and civil religion
secular.author: Sociologists of American religion
secular.whatItGetsRight: The students of American civil religion exposed how easily the symbols of the faith get fused with the symbols of the nation, how a vague God is enlisted to bless the tribe and sanctify the flag, and how this fusion serves power while emptying the gospel of its content. They named the real and present danger of a Christianity that has become the chaplain of a political movement, that confuses the Kingdom of God with a particular nation or party, and that wields the cross as a tribal banner. This is precisely the idolatry the two cities doctrine was built to expose.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The critics see the idolatry clearly and, in some hands, replace one capture with another, denouncing the fusion of faith and nation on the right while quietly fusing faith and ideology on the left, so that the church is told to abandon one party's mascot only to adopt the other's. Scripture rebukes every fusion, for Joshua learned that God is on neither side but summons both to his, and the prophets indicted the people of God before they indicted the nations. The corrective the critics offer is real and needs its own corrective, that the answer to a captured faith is not a faith captured by the opposite party, but a faith captured by Christ alone, free to indict the idolatry of every tribe including the critic's own.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same Lord and the same first allegiance to his Kingdom still differ on how the believer should engage the earthly city, and the difference is not careless. It runs to whether the church is called to transform the public order from within or to bear a distinct witness from a healthy distance. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are reading the same Scripture that commands the welfare of the city and warns against the worship of it, and both are guarding against a real danger.

views.view: The church is called to engage and shape the public order for the common good
views.body: This view holds that the lordship of Christ extends over every sphere, including the political, and that to seek the welfare of the city means active and faithful participation in its public life, in voting, governing, advocacy, and the patient work of bending a society's laws and structures toward justice and the common good. The model is Joseph and Daniel serving in pagan governments, the prophets confronting kings, Jeremiah's command to seek the city's welfare, the church building hospitals and schools and reforming unjust laws across the centuries. Advocates argue that to retreat from public life is to abandon the neighbor to whatever powers happen to rule, that love requires the believer to care whether the structures of his society honor or destroy the vulnerable, and that the salt does no good in the shaker. They warn that a church which withdraws from the public square in the name of purity simply hands the square to the worst actors and then complains about the result. The danger they are guarding against is a privatized and irresponsible faith that washes its hands of the common life, that lets injustice roll on while it tends its own garden, and that mistakes its absence for holiness. Against that they hold that the believer is sent into the city to seek its good with both hands, engaged and faithful, working for justice while keeping his first allegiance clear, neither fleeing the public square nor worshiping it.

views.view: The church bears its truest political witness by being a distinct community, not by seizing the levers of power
views.body: This view holds that the church's first and most powerful political act is to be the church, a community whose common life across every human division shows the world an alternative to the politics of the tribe, and that the constant temptation to capture the levers of state power tends to corrupt the witness it means to serve. The model is the early church that conquered the empire not by winning elections but by living and dying differently, the Anabaptist refusal to wield the sword, the Confessing Church that resisted by simply being the church against the captured one. Advocates argue that whenever the church has grasped for political power it has compromised its gospel, baptized the empire, and become a chaplain to whoever was winning, and that its real influence has always flowed from its strange and faithful common life rather than from its grip on office. They warn that the lust to transform society through power is the very thing that has repeatedly captured and corrupted the church, turning it into one more tribe fighting for control. The danger they are guarding against is a triumphalist faith that confuses winning elections with advancing the Kingdom, that will compromise anything for a seat at the table, and that loses its soul in the bargain. Against that they hold that the church changes the world most by refusing to be conformed to it, that its politics is its peoplehood, and that a community which loves across the lines everyone else defends is a louder sermon than any law it could pass.

parts.title: What Citizenship Under Christ Forms in You
parts.body:
You do not become free of partisan capture by trying harder to be balanced. The Bible is after something the voter guide cannot reach, a person whose deepest loyalty has been so firmly fixed on the Kingdom that every earthly allegiance falls into its proper, smaller place, and the fixing is the point, because politics is not finally a problem you solve but a fire that reveals which city your heart actually loves.

He forms in you a settled freedom from the desperation of the tribe. The man whose whole hope rides on the earthly city must win at any cost, because for him the election really is the last judgment, and so he will lie, hate, and justify any means. The believer whose hope is fixed in the heavenly city is free, free to lose without despair, free to be fair to his opponent, free to tell the truth even when it wounds his own side, because he already knows how the real story ends. This freedom is not apathy. It is the calm of a citizen who serves the city with both hands precisely because he has stopped worshiping it.

He forms in you the capacity to love across the line. The partisan age trains you to see the people on the other side as enemies, fools, or threats, and the gospel slowly dismantles the training, because the man across the political divide is your neighbor and may be your brother, bought by the same blood, owed the same love. To sit at one table with someone whose politics you oppose, and to love them genuinely, is one of the most countercultural acts available in a polarized society, and it is the very thing the church was made to display. The believer becomes a person whose love cannot be predicted from his politics, and that unpredictability is itself a witness.

He forms in you a prophetic distance from your own side. The captured Christian can see only the sins of the other tribe. The free Christian, formed by the prophets who indicted Israel first, becomes able to name the idolatry, the cruelty, and the self-deception of his own party, to refuse the slogan his side hands him, to grow quiet when his tribe is wrong instead of loud only when his opponents are. This is the hardest formation of all, because it costs him the warmth of belonging, and it is the truest mark that Christ and not the party now holds the throne.

And he forms in you the likeness of the King who entered the city he came to save and refused every shortcut to power. They offered Jesus all the kingdoms of the world if he would only worship the wrong lord, and he refused. They wanted to make him king by force, and he withdrew. He rode into Jerusalem not on a war horse but on a donkey, and took a cross instead of a throne, and conquered by losing in a way no earthly politics can comprehend. This is the King the Christian citizen serves, and as his Spirit works down into the muscle of an ordinary public life, you become a person who can hold your citizenship in an open hand, loyal to the city and unowned by it, working for its welfare while your whole heart belongs, finally and freely, to another country that no party can deliver and no election can take away.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: Freedom from political idolatry is not a position you adopt. It is a set of practices you take up, in small repeated acts, until the first allegiance becomes a reflex and the tribe loses its grip on your heart. None of what follows will resolve the issues or tell you how to vote, and none of it will purge the partisan out of you by Friday. All of it will start to wear a groove if you keep at it. Begin where you are, with one thing, this week.

steps: Notice where your political heat is greater than your gospel heat, and confess it. Track what you scroll, what raises your pulse, what you would actually argue about at the table, and ask honestly which throne your heart is serving.

Read Jeremiah 29 and ask what it would mean to seek the welfare of the actual city where God has put you, including the neighbors who vote against you. Let the command to bless Babylon dismantle both your reflexes.

Name one sin your own political tribe has made its peace with, out loud, and feel how much harder it is than naming the other side's. The captured heart can only see the enemy's sins. Begin the cure by seeing your own.

Pray for a leader you did not vote for, by name, the way Paul told the church to pray for the emperor who was Nero. Notice what it does to your heart to ask God's good for someone your tribe calls the enemy.

Share a real meal with a brother or sister whose politics you oppose, and refuse to let the politics rise like a wall. Stay at the table long enough to remember that you are family before you are factions.

Read the prophets indicting Israel, not the nations, and let them teach you to hear judgment begin with the household of God. Apply one of their indictments to your own side before you apply any to the other.

Fast from the outrage machine for the month, the cable, the feeds, the voices that exist to convince you the other side is evil. Notice how much of your political certainty was manufactured by people paid to keep you angry.

Find one issue where the Bible cuts against your party's whole position, and sit with it honestly instead of explaining it away. Let the Scripture be larger than the slogan, and let it cost you a settled certainty.

Read Augustine on the two cities, or a faithful guide to it, until the distinction is in your bones, so that you can love the earthly city without confusing it with the Kingdom and serve it without staking your soul on it.

Examine your church's witness. Can an outsider predict everything you believe about God and mercy from the way the congregation votes. Have one honest conversation with your leaders about whether the body has been sorted by party.

Build one bridge across the divide that costs you something, a friendship, a partnership for the common good, a shared work for the welfare of your actual city pursued alongside people you disagree with politically. Let the common good outrank the tribe.

Memorize the heart of the matter until it governs you. Render to God the things that are God's. Are you for us or for our adversaries. No, but as commander of the Lord's army I have come. Seek the welfare of the city. Let these dismantle the capture from inside.

Cultivate, over years, a public faith that no party can claim, so that your votes follow your convictions and your convictions follow Scripture, and the watching world cannot read your gospel off your ballot.

Take up one long obedience for the common good that outlasts every election cycle, a work for the welfare of your city, the vulnerable, the place God has put you, kept faithfully whichever tribe is winning at the moment.

Be the kind of Christian who can be trusted to tell his own side the truth, formed by the prophets to name the idolatry of his own tribe, free of the desperation that turns politics into worship, loyal to the city and unowned by it.

Keep returning to the King who refused the kingdoms of the world and took a cross instead of a throne. Read his politics for the rest of your life not as a strategy to win but as a window onto the Lord who conquered by losing, until your citizenship in his Kingdom and your love for your earthly city have found, in you, their right and lasting order.
